examples.question_text: A differentiable curve has a stationary point at $P$. What is the gradient of its tangent at $P$?
examples.solution_text: At a stationary point, the first derivative is zero. The tangent at $P$ is horizontal, with gradient $0$.

examples.question_text: Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $y=2x^2-12x+7$.
examples.solution_text:
$y'=4x-12$.

Set $y'=0$:
$\begin{aligned}4x-12&=0\\4x&=12\\x&=3\end{aligned}$

Substitute into the original function:
$\begin{aligned}y&=2(3)^2-12(3)+7\\&=-11\end{aligned}$

The stationary point is $(3,-11)$.

$f'(x)=3x^2-6x-9$.

Set $f'(x)=0$:
$\begin{aligned}3x^2-6x-9&=0\\3(x-3)(x+1)&=0\\x&=-1\text{ or }3\end{aligned}$

Substitute into the original function:
$\begin{aligned}f(-1)&=(-1)^3-3(-1)^2-9(-1)+4\\&=9\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}f(3)&=3^3-3(3)^2-9(3)+4\\&=-23\end{aligned}$

The stationary points are $(-1,9)$ and $(3,-23)$.

examples.question_text: Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $y=(x+2)^3-1$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $y=(x+1)^4+2$.
Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $f(x)=x^4-108x+5$.

examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}y'&=12x^3-24x^2\\&=12x^2(x-2)\end{aligned}$

Set $y'=0$:
$\begin{aligned}12x^2(x-2)&=0\\x&=0\text{ or }2\end{aligned}$

$y(0)=6$.

$\begin{aligned}y(2)&=3(2)^4-8(2)^3+6\\&=-10\end{aligned}$

The stationary points are $(0,6)$ and $(2,-10)$.

examples.question_text: Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $y=x+\dfrac{16}{x}$ for $x>0$.
examples.solution_text:
Write the reciprocal as a negative power:
$y=x+16x^{-1}$.

$\begin{aligned}y'&=1-16x^{-2}\\&=1-\dfrac{16}{x^2}\end{aligned}$

Set $y'=0$:
$\begin{aligned}1-\dfrac{16}{x^2}&=0\\x^2&=16\end{aligned}$

Since $x>0$, $x=4$.

$\begin{aligned}y&=4+\dfrac{16}{4}\\&=8\end{aligned}$

The stationary point is $(4,8)$.

examples.question_text: Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $y=\dfrac{x-3}{x^2}$, where $x\ne0$.
examples.solution_text:
Use the quotient rule:
$\begin{aligned}y'&=\dfrac{x^2-(x-3)(2x)}{x^4}\\&=\dfrac{-x^2+6x}{x^4}\\&=\dfrac{6-x}{x^3}\end{aligned}$

A fraction is zero when its numerator is zero and its denominator is nonzero. Set $y'=0$:
$\begin{aligned}6-x&=0\\x&=6\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}y&=\dfrac{6-3}{6^2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{12}\end{aligned}$

The stationary point is $\left(6,\dfrac{1}{12}\right)$.

examples.question_text: For what values of $k$ does $f(x)=x^3+kx^2+27x+2$ have no stationary points?
examples.solution_text:
$f'(x)=3x^2+2kx+27$.

There are no stationary points when $f'(x)=0$ has no real roots. Its discriminant must be negative:
$\begin{aligned}(2k)^2-4(3)(27)&<0\\4k^2-324&<0\\k^2&<81\\-9&<k<9\end{aligned}$

At $k=-9$ or $k=9$, the derivative has a repeated real root and a stationary point exists. Both endpoints are excluded.

examples.derivation: The definition of a stationary point gives f'(P)=0, so its tangent is horizontal with gradient 0.
y'=4x-12 vanishes only at x=3. Substitution gives y=18-36+7=-11, so the stationary point is (3,-11).
y'=3(x+2)² vanishes only at x=-2, where y=-1. The plotted expression is the original cubic; its marked point, dashed projection and horizontal tangent agree. Both axes intersect at the origin.
y'=4(x+1)³=0 gives x=-1. The original function gives y=2, so the unique stationary point is (-1,2).
y'=12x³-24x²=12x²(x-2), whose distinct roots are 0 and 2. Substitution gives y(0)=6 and y(2)=48-64+6=-10; both stationary points are retained.
Writing y=x+16x⁻¹ gives y'=1-16/x². Its zeros satisfy x²=16; the stated positive domain retains x=4 only. Then y=4+16/4=8.
The quotient rule gives y'=[x²-2x(x-3)]/x⁴=(6-x)/x³ for x≠0. Its numerator vanishes at x=6, an allowed value. Substitution gives y=3/36=1/12.
f'(x)=3x²+2kx+27 has no real zero exactly when its discriminant 4k²-324 is negative, giving -9<k<9. At either endpoint the repeated derivative root produces a stationary point.
